subtitle: The Profession · Ethics · Systems · Problem Framing

blocks.narration: Welcome to the complete video guide to Introduction to Engineering, weeks one to four. Over the next half hour we answer four questions. What is an engineer, and how is engineering different from science, design, and repair? What is a system, a boundary, a stakeholder? How do you draw a process flow diagram? And how do you turn a vague complaint into a measurable engineering problem? Everything comes from the course guide — walk into the test ready.

blocks.title: Engineering as a Profession
blocks.subtitle: From ingenium to the modern discipline
blocks.narration: Chapter one. Before any diagram or formula, the course asks a simpler question: what is an engineer? We cover the word itself, the classical fields, the profession's roles in history and society, and the famous triad — science, design, and engineering. It is the base for everything that follows.

blocks.heading: What Is an Engineer?
bullets: Latin ingenium — a talented invention
ingeniare — to devise, to invent
a creative, inventive problem solver
engineering is design — not repair
blocks.narration: The word engineer comes from the Latin ingenium — the fruit of genius, a talented invention — and the verb ingeniare, to devise, to invent. Two thousand years ago it named the design of new machines — then the machines, then their designers. The course definition: an engineer is a creative, inventive person who finds solutions to practical problems. Engineering uses natural science, mathematics, and the design process to solve technical problems and improve systems. And a favorite exam point: engineering is not repair. A plumber fixes pipes; an engineer designs the water system — diameters, pressures, layouts — before anything is built.

blocks.heading: Fields of Engineering and Their Societies
blocks.narration: The lecture lists eight classical fields — and each has its professional society, so learn the pairs. ASME is mechanical engineering; IEEE unites electrical and computer engineers; ASCE is civil — roads, bridges, water systems; AIChE is chemical; AIAA is aerospace; ANS is nuclear. Beyond them sit biomedical, environmental, agricultural, marine, materials, and textile engineering; Kosky adds ASTM for materials and BMES for biomedical. A typical society defines its disciplines, sets codes and standards, offers continuing education, and keeps its own code of ethics. A historical note: the oldest engineering is military — the first non-military engineers were called civilians, later civil engineers.

blocks.heading: Roles, Numbers and Traits
bullets: four eras: steam, electricity, flight, computing
engineers sit between science and society
over 1.6 million engineers in the USA
ten traits — a team needs a mix
blocks.narration: Four eras mark the profession's history: the Industrial Revolution, electrification, the age of aviation and the automobile, and the digital age. In each, engineers turned new science into infrastructure people use. Gordon Stanley Brown of MIT said it best: engineers sit at the interface between science and society. The economics: over one point six million engineers work in the United States — the second-largest profession — with a starting salary near sixty-eight thousand dollars, and fourteen Grand Challenges from clean water to solar energy. And the ten traits of the problem solver: objective, analytical, creative, dedicated, curious, courageous, adventurous, enthusiastic, patient, vigilant. Teams are formed with a mix — five Objective members argue forever.

blocks.heading: Science, Design and Engineering
bullets: science asks: why does this happen?
engineering asks: how do we make it work?
design gives the solution its form
engineering design: form disciplined by analysis
blocks.narration: The week's triad. Science investigates what already exists and asks why does this happen. Engineering creates what has never existed and asks how do we make it work, under real constraints. Design is the creative act of giving a solution its form — shape, aesthetics, user experience. Engineering design is design disciplined by analysis: physics, materials, cost, and safety constrain the possibilities. The bridge test: a striking shape with no regard for load bearing is design without engineering; a shape derived from an analysis of loads is engineering design. As Steve Jobs put it: design is not how it looks and feels — design is how it works.

blocks.heading: Sort the Card: Science, Engineering, Design?
blocks.problem: Four cards from Lab 1 — sort each into Science, Engineering, Design, or Overlap.

steps.text: Study why a bridge sagged — Science
Design a bridge truss for the load — Engineering
Choose the color and shape — Design

blocks.result: Tie-breaker: shape? with or without constraints?
blocks.narration: Here is how the lab's sorting game works. Card one: study why a bridge sagged. That investigates what already exists — Science. Card two: design a bridge truss for the load — Engineering, creating something new under hard constraints. Card three: choose the color and shape of a car body. It gives form without mandatory technical constraints — Design. Card four: a body shape optimized for aerodynamics and safety — the overlap again, design disciplined by physics. The lab's tie-breaker question: does the card take part in giving shape or appearance? If no — engineering. If yes, without technical constraints — design. If yes, and with constraints — the overlap.

items: engineer: a creative solver of practical problems
engineering is design and analysis — not repair
eight classical fields; six key societies
science asks why; engineering asks how
a team needs a mix of traits
blocks.narration: Chapter one in five lines. An engineer is a creative, inventive solver of practical problems — from the Latin ingenium. Engineering is design and analysis before anything breaks, never repair. Eight classical fields, each with its society — ASME, IEEE, ASCE, and the rest. Science asks why, engineering asks how, design gives form. And a team needs a mix of traits — five clones of one trait solve nothing.

blocks.title: Engineering Ethics
blocks.subtitle: The NSPE canons and personal ethics
blocks.narration: Chapter two. Engineering decisions touch safety, health, and money — so the profession polices itself with codes of ethics. We cover the NSPE fundamental canons, the lab's ten canons, the five cornerstones of personal ethics, and the decision matrix that turns a dilemma into a table.

blocks.heading: The Six NSPE Fundamental Canons
rows: Hold paramount public safety and welfare
Act as faithful agents or trustees
blocks.narration: The fundamental canons of the National Society of Professional Engineers, in full. One: hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public. Two: perform services only in areas of your competence. Three: issue public statements only in an objective and truthful manner. Four: act for each employer or client as a faithful agent or trustee. Five: avoid deceptive acts. Six: conduct yourself honorably, responsibly, ethically, and lawfully, to enhance the honor and usefulness of the profession. Canon one overrides everything: when safety conflicts with business, safety wins. Together the canons protect all four stakeholders — the public, the client, the profession, and the engineer.

blocks.heading: Why a Code — and the Ten Canons of the Lab
bullets: serves society, employer, profession, self
protects against pressure to cut corners
lab adds: credit, no hidden payments, speak up
blocks.narration: A professional code of ethics ensures the profession serves the legitimate purposes of all stakeholders — oneself, the employer, the profession, and society — and protects engineers from the pressure to cut corners for the sake of savings. Armed with the code, an engineer can say: I cannot place business interests above professional ethics. Lab 1 adapts the canons into ten short formulations, the convenient ones to memorize: safety first; stay in your lane; speak truthfully; no conflicts of interest; no deception; act honorably. Then four more: no hidden payments from several parties; never misrepresent your qualifications; give proper credit; and do not stay silent — report violations even under pressure.

blocks.heading: The Five Cornerstones of Personal Ethics
bullets: do what you say you will do
keep confidences; take responsibility
never take part in a lie
never accept compromising gifts
blocks.narration: Beyond the professional code, Kosky lists five cornerstones of personal ethical behavior. First, do what you say you will do. Second, never disclose information given to you in confidence. Third, take responsibility for your actions and your mistakes. Fourth, never participate in a lie. Fifth, never accept gifts that would compromise your ability to act in your organization's best interests. Kosky admits the list is incomplete — it lacks the golden rule: do not do to others what you do not wish for yourself, in Confucius's version. And the top question of a personal decision: would I do this in front of my mother? If not — do not.

blocks.heading: The Engineering Ethics Decision Matrix
bullets: rows: the canons; columns: actions
each cell: yes, no, or maybe
sum the yes and no per column
one criterion can override the count
blocks.narration: The course's main ethical tool: the Engineering Ethics Decision Matrix. The rows are the NSPE canons. The columns are courses of action — go along, appeal to upper management, resign, or call a journalist. Each cell answers one question: does this course of action satisfy this canon? Yes, no, or maybe. Then sum the yes and no answers down each column, ignoring the maybes — the count suggests the first action. Its value is divide and conquer: it forces all the dimensions into view, instead of the first yes or no that comes to mind. One exception: if a single criterion — public safety — overrides all the others, follow it, whatever the count says.

blocks.heading: Case: The Roommate and the Homework
blocks.problem: Your roommate partied all weekend and asks to see your homework before class. What do you do?

steps.text: Do what you say: showing it breaks your word
Do not take part in a lie

blocks.narration: Kosky's canonical case from the lecture and Lab 1. Your roommate spent the weekend partying and asks to see your homework before class. Run it through the cornerstones. Do what you say: an individual assignment implicitly promises the work is yours — showing it breaks that promise. Confidentiality: homework is private communication between student and instructor. Responsibility: letting someone copy makes you an accomplice. And do not participate in a lie: copied work submitted as one's own is a lie. The fifth cornerstone, gifts, does not apply. Four of five support refusal; the golden rule adds empathy: refuse, but offer to help them understand and do the work together. Under the university code, a first violation means zero for the assignment.

blocks.heading: The Ethics Courtroom: The Electrical Plan
blocks.problem: A civil engineer is asked to sign a building's electrical wiring plan — he is the only one free right now, but he has never studied electrical systems.

steps.text: Route the work to an electrical engineer

blocks.narration: From Lab 1's Ethics Courtroom. A civil engineer is asked to sign the electrical wiring plan of a building — he is the only one free right now, but he has never studied electrical systems. The verdict: decline, and route the work to a qualified electrical engineer. The canon: number two — perform services only in areas of your competence. A signature under an unsound plan also violates canon one, public safety, and canon eight, misrepresenting your qualifications. Note the game's answer format: verdict plus canon number, then supporting arguments. Every case in the game is solved the same way — find the canon the request breaks, and refuse professionally, with reasons.

items: canon 1: public safety above all
ten canons: from safety first to speak up
five cornerstones plus the golden rule
matrix: canons times actions — count yes and no
blocks.narration: Ethics in four lines. Canon one holds the safety, health, and welfare of the public above everything. The lab's ten canons run from safety first to do not stay silent. Personal ethics rests on five cornerstones, plus the golden rule. And the decision matrix multiplies canons by courses of action — count the yes and no answers, and let safety override the count when it must.

chapters.title: Systems Thinking I: Systems and Boundaries

blocks.title: Systems Thinking I
blocks.subtitle: Systems, boundaries, stakeholders
blocks.narration: Chapter three. Week two shifts the view: instead of the profession, we look at how engineers see the world — as systems. You will learn the definition of a system, why a pile of parts is not one, how to draw the boundary, what an operating context is, and how to map stakeholders.

blocks.heading: What Is a System?
bullets: interacting elements and processes
transform inputs into outputs
exists within an operating context
blocks.narration: The key definition of the week: a system is a set of interacting elements and processes that transform inputs into outputs and exist within an operating context. Four parts, and each earns its place. Elements are the parts and the people that make up the system. Processes are how the parts interact and transform things over time. Inputs and outputs are what flows in and what flows out. And the operating context is the set of conditions under which the system exists. Keep the four parts together — they are the checklist the course returns to every week, from the cafeteria to the solar panel line.

blocks.heading: A System Is Not a Pile of Parts
bullets: a pile of bricks is not a wall
parts must interact, with a purpose
wall = bricks + mortar + a load path
blocks.narration: A random heap of parts is not a system. A system is parts with a purpose, connected so they act together, not merely lie together. A pile of bricks in the yard — against a brick wall: bricks, mortar, and a load path holding the weight. A student, a timetable, a bus stop — against a bus route, where vehicles, schedule, and passengers interact to move people. A stove, a refrigerator, a sink — against a cafeteria kitchen, where staff, equipment, and workflow turn ingredients into meals. A phone, a bank, a shop with no link — against a payment app tying accounts, verification, transfer into one flow.

blocks.heading: The Boundary and the Operating Context
bullets: a line between inside and outside
the boundary is drawn, not discovered
context: codes, schedule, infrastructure, budget
blocks.narration: The system boundary is a drawn line, often imaginary, separating inside from outside; materials, people, money, information, and energy may cross it. The key idea of the week: the boundary is an engineer's choice, not a fact about the world. Two engineers may draw the same system differently; both are right if the choice is justified and consistent. Just outside sits the operating context: conditions that never cross as inputs yet still constrain the system — codes and standards, schedule, infrastructure, budget and resources. For the cafeteria: inputs — food deliveries, staff, students; outputs — meals, waste, payments; context — sanitary code, opening hours, kitchen budget, building layout.

blocks.heading: Stakeholders and Tensions
bullets: uses it; runs it; affected by it
a first draft is enough to start
stakeholders want different things
blocks.narration: A stakeholder is anyone who uses the system, runs it, or is affected by it — whether or not they sit inside the boundary. The stakeholder map has three columns: uses it, like students eating in the cafeteria; runs it, like kitchen staff, dispatchers, and maintenance crews; affected by it, like the neighbors living with the noise — often entirely outside the boundary. A first draft is enough to get started. The important part: stakeholders do not always want the same thing. For the bus route, the university wants it faster, the maintenance crew safer, the passengers cheaper. Good systems thinking notices the tension instead of hiding it.

blocks.heading: The Stakeholder Map
blocks.narration: Here is the map as a table, for three systems. The campus cafeteria: uses it — students eating lunch; runs it — kitchen staff; affected by it — neighbors with the noise. The bus route: uses it — passengers; runs it — drivers and dispatchers; affected by it — people on the street. The charging station from Lab 2: uses it — drivers of electric cars; runs it — facilities and maintenance; affected by it — the neighboring offices. Draft the table, mark where the wants collide — that is Milestone one's third deliverable. Remember: neighbors and offices sit outside the boundary — and still count.

blocks.heading: System or Just a Collection?
blocks.problem: Classify: (a) a pile of bricks; (b) a bus route; (c) kitchen appliances; (d) a payment app.

steps.text: (a) a pile of bricks — not a system
(b) a bus route — vehicles, schedule, passengers

blocks.narration: The lecture's classification quiz, with model answers. A pile of bricks: not a system — parts lie around with no connection and no purpose. A bus route: a system — vehicles, schedule, and passengers interact to move people. Kitchen appliances on their own: not a system — but the cafeteria kitchen, with staff and a workflow, is. A payment app: the phone, the bank, and the shop are not a system separately, but the app ties accounts, verification, and transfer into one flow — a system. The criterion is the same: interacting elements and processes transforming inputs into outputs, for a purpose. If yes, draw the boundary and call it a system.

items: system: elements, processes, inputs, outputs, context
the boundary is drawn, not discovered
context: codes, schedule, infrastructure, budget
stakeholders: uses it, runs it, affected by it
surface the tension — do not hide it
blocks.narration: Week two in five lines. A system is interacting elements and processes turning inputs into outputs inside an operating context. The boundary is drawn, not discovered. The context is codes, schedule, infrastructure, budget. Stakeholders use it, run it, or are affected by it. And when wants collide, surface the tension — it is a property of the system, not a flaw in your map.

chapters.title: Systems Thinking II: Process Flow Diagrams

blocks.title: Systems Thinking II: Process Flow Diagrams
blocks.subtitle: What happens inside the boundary
blocks.narration: Chapter four. Week three opens the black box: a process flow diagram shows the steps of a process in order and what flows between them. You will learn the three levels of detail, five symbols, five rules, five kinds of flow — and why the same system looks different through different eyes.

blocks.heading: What a Process Flow Diagram Gives You
bullets: the sequence: first, next, last
the flow: what moves between steps
the problems: gaps, waits, loops, hand-offs
elements are nouns; processes are verbs
blocks.narration: A process flow diagram — a PFD — shows the steps of a process in order, and what flows between them. Three things it gives you: the sequence, what happens first, next, and last; the flow, what moves between the steps; and the problems — gaps, waits, loops, and hand-offs become visible on paper. The cafeteria's elements are the nouns — cooks, ovens, trays, tables, students; its processes are the verbs — receive, store, prepare, serve, take payment, clear. Week two listed the parts; the PFD shows what they do together. Kosky even draws the design process itself this way: the design process is a process too.

blocks.heading: Three Levels of Detail
bullets: Level 0: black box — only inputs and outputs
Level 1: the main steps inside
Level 2: zoom into one step
one level per diagram
blocks.narration: One process, three levels of detail — choose the level that fits the question, and keep one level per diagram. Level zero, the black box: inputs come in, outputs go out, the inside is hidden. For the cafeteria: food, staff, and students in; meals, waste, and payments out. Level one, the main steps: receive deliveries, store ingredients, prepare meals, serve meals, take payment, clear and dispose. Level two, the zoom: one step expanded into its own diagram — prepare meals becomes wash, chop, cook, hold hot. Compare level one with level zero and you see exactly where each flow enters: deliveries at step one, students at step four, payments leaving at step five.

blocks.heading: Five Symbols — and Five Rules
rows: where the process begins and ends
a question with Yes and No exits
an arrow: order, and what moves
a dashed box where things wait
blocks.narration: Five symbols — five are enough. Start and end mark the beginning and the end; one start, every path reaches an end. A step is a single action, named verb plus noun — receive deliveries, not delivery. A decision is a diamond with labeled yes and no exits. A flow is an arrow: the order of the steps, and what moves along them. A wait, or queue, is a dashed box where things wait. And five rules keep it readable: start and end explicitly; steps verb plus noun; label every arrow; both exits at every decision; one level of detail — boundary-crossing arrows are your inputs and outputs. The reader should never have to guess.

blocks.heading: Every Arrow Carries Something
bullets: material, people, information, money, energy
the label shows what the next step needs
queues and decisions slow the system down
blocks.narration: Every arrow carries something, in one of five categories — the same five as the week-two inputs and outputs. Material: ingredients, trays, food waste. People: students in a queue. Information: menus, orders, meal-plan verification. Money: payments, supplier bills. Energy: gas, electricity, hot water. The label shows what the next step needs. A dashed box marks a wait, a diamond marks a choice: food available — yes, take payment; no, prepare more meals, back to step three. Queues and decisions are where systems slow down. And in the swimlane version the diagram splits by performer — student, kitchen staff, cashier — and every hand-off between lanes is a place where delays and errors hide.

blocks.heading: A Diagram Is a Model with a Purpose
bullets: Beck's Underground map, the early 1930s
keeps: stations, lines, interchanges
drops: distances, street geography
blocks.narration: Harry Beck's London Underground map of the early nineteen thirties drops distances and street geography, keeps stations, lines, interchanges. Every diagram keeps what serves the purpose and drops the rest — that is why it works. And the same system looks different through five pairs of eyes. The rider waits, boards, rides — success is a short wait and a low fare. The driver checks the bus and runs the route — success is a workable schedule. Maintenance inspects, repairs, returns to service. The administration sets budget and timetable, reviews ridership. The neighbor hears the bus and notices the traffic. Different boundaries, steps, definitions of success — none is wrong. Good engineers draw several and ask: whose view is missing?

blocks.heading: Fix the Diagram
blocks.problem: Find at least four errors: Kitchen — Students enter — Food available? (Yes) — Chop onions — Serve meals — Pay

steps.text: Decision has only a Yes exit — add No
Label the arrows: students, meals, money

blocks.result: Five errors — the reader should never guess
blocks.narration: The lecture's find-the-errors walkthrough. The broken diagram runs: kitchen, students enter, food available — yes, chop onions, serve meals, pay. Error one: no start and end symbols — add them. Error two: kitchen is a place, not a step — rename it prepare meals. Error three: the decision has only a yes exit — add no: prepare more meals, with an arrow back. Error four: chop onions is level-two detail inside a level-one diagram — keep one level. Error five: the arrows are unlabeled — label what moves: students, meals, money. Five errors; the key accepts four or more. The rules matter: the reader should never have to guess — a diagram that must be decoded will be misread.

items: PFD = steps in order + flows between them
levels 0, 1, 2 — one level per diagram
5 symbols; 5 rules; 5 kinds of flow
label every arrow — the reader must not guess
each stakeholder draws a different map
blocks.narration: Week three in five lines. A PFD shows the steps in order and what flows between them. Three levels: black box, main steps, zoom — one level per diagram. Five symbols, five rules, five kinds of flow. Label every arrow, because the reader must never guess. And the same system looks different through each stakeholder's eyes — ask whose view is missing.

chapters.title: Numbers on the Arrows: Units and Mass Balance

blocks.title: Numbers on the Arrows
blocks.subtitle: Variables, units, significant figures
blocks.narration: Chapter five. Diagrams show structure; engineering also needs numbers. This chapter covers variables and units, the SI system, Kosky's bracket method for conversions, significant figures, and the mass balance — the tool that puts numbers on the arrows. The story includes a lost spacecraft.

blocks.heading: A Variable Is a Number Plus Units
bullets: a quantity that can be measured
dimensions: mass, length, time, temperature
units give the numerical scale
blocks.formula_caption: read: speed equals distance divided by time
blocks.narration: An engineering calculation is not a purely mathematical one — a single number is not enough. The result must be right in four ways: right variables, correct value, correct units, correct significant figures. A variable is a measurable quantity: how hot — temperature; how heavy — weight; what voltage — electrical potential. Dimensions are the fundamental quantities we perceive — mass, length, time; units give the numerical scale. Speed is a ruler measurement over a clock measurement: speed equals distance divided by time. Units matter: one hundred on a Canadian speeding ticket is one hundred kilometers per hour — only sixty-two miles per hour. A number without units is incomplete.

blocks.heading: Derived SI Units
blocks.narration: The SI system is the metric standard, built on the meter, kilogram, and second, with the kelvin, mole, and ampere — and the candela as the seventh base unit. From them come the derived units in this table. Force is the newton — the force that accelerates one kilogram at one meter per second squared. Energy is the joule, a newton-meter. Power is the watt, one joule per second. Charge is the coulomb, an ampere-second. Potential is the volt, a watt per ampere. Pressure is the pascal, a newton per square meter. Hertz, ohm, and farad complete the family.

blocks.heading: Writing Units and Significant Figures
bullets: names lowercase; symbols from names capitalized
never plural, never a period
brackets on every quantity: 12 [in/ft]
significant figures: match the least precise
blocks.formula_caption: read: ten feet times twelve inches per foot equals one hundred twenty inches
blocks.narration: Kosky's rules: unit names are lowercase — newton, joule; abbreviations from a person's name are capitalized — N, J. Abbreviations take no plural and no period; a second letter appears only to avoid confusion — Wb for weber, against W for watt. For conversions, the fail-safe method: units in square brackets on every quantity, canceling like fractions — ten feet times twelve inches per foot gives one hundred twenty inches; the final answer carries no brackets. And significant figures: for sums, the result stops at the decimal position of the least precise number; for products, it carries no more digits than the least precise factor; round only the final answer — zero to four stays, five to nine raises.

blocks.heading: The Mars Climate Orbiter
blocks.problem: Launched 11 December 1998; lost 23 September 1999. What went wrong?

steps.text: Entry at 57 km instead of 140–150 km

blocks.result: Check unit consistency across the system
blocks.narration: The cautionary case of the course. The Mars Climate Orbiter was launched on December eleventh, nineteen ninety-eight, and lost on September twenty-third, nineteen ninety-nine, while entering orbit at Mars. The commission concluded that the engineers failed to convert the rocket thrust from pounds-force to newtons — the units the navigation software expected. The spacecraft entered the Martian atmosphere at about fifty-seven kilometers instead of the planned one hundred forty to one hundred fifty kilometers, and was destroyed. The lesson in one sentence: inconsistent units kill missions. The model answer adds: fix the process — audit the software and check unit consistency across the whole design, not just find a culprit.

blocks.heading: Concentration: How Pollution Is Measured
bullets: concentration: mass per unit volume
water: 1 ppm = 1 mg/L; 1 ppb = 1 μg/L
air: ppm × molar mass ÷ 24.45
blocks.formula_caption: read: the concentration of A equals the mass of A divided by the volume of the mixture
blocks.narration: Environmental engineering measures pollution by concentration — the mass of a pollutant per unit volume of the mixture. The formula: concentration equals mass divided by the volume of the mixture. For water, one part per million equals one milligram per liter; one part per billion, one microgram per liter. The lecture's image: one cup of pollutant in a swimming pool is parts per million; one drop is parts per billion. Air is standardized at one atmosphere and twenty-five degrees Celsius, where the molar volume is twenty-four point four five liters per mole — so milligrams per cubic meter equal parts per million times molar mass over twenty-four point four five.

blocks.heading: The Mass Balance Equation

parts.note: accumulation: mass stored in the control volume
generated or destroyed inside by reactions

blocks.narration: The main tool: the mass balance. In words: mass accumulated equals mass in, minus mass out, plus mass created or destroyed inside. The rate form is on screen. In yellow, on the left: the accumulation rate, how fast mass is stored inside the control volume. In blue: the sum of incoming mass flow rates. In green: the sum of outgoing ones. In red: the generation rate — mass of a chemical species created or destroyed by reactions. Mass itself is never created or destroyed, except in nuclear reactions — but a species can be, when reactions transform it. And the powerful special case: no accumulation, no reactions — input simply equals output.

blocks.heading: The Transfer Center
blocks.problem: A Transfer Center receives 600 tons of waste per day from community A and 400 from B; 25% is recycled; the incinerator burns 200 tons per day. How much goes to the landfill?

steps.text: Need: the disposal rate to the landfill

blocks.narration: Kosky's example eighteen point two, from lecture three. A Transfer Center receives six hundred tons of waste per day from one community and four hundred from another. Twenty-five percent is recycled, and the incinerator burns two hundred tons per day. How much must go to the landfill? Set it up with the method. Need: the disposal rate to the landfill. Know: the mass flow rates at input and output. How: the Transfer Center as a control volume, apply the balance. Solve: no reactions, so generation is zero; nothing accumulates — input equals output. One thousand in; two hundred fifty recycled plus two hundred burned plus the landfill flow out. The landfill receives five hundred fifty tons per day.

items: a variable = a number + its units
right in four ways: variables, value, units, figures
brackets on quantities; units cancel
concentration: mass per volume; ppm and ppb
no accumulation, no reactions: input = output
blocks.narration: The quantitative toolkit in five lines. A variable is a number plus its units — both must be right, with the significant figures. Write units in brackets and let them cancel. Concentration is mass per volume — parts per million, milligrams per liter. And the mass balance: no accumulation, no reactions — input equals output; one thousand minus two hundred fifty minus two hundred leaves five hundred fifty tons a day.

blocks.title: Problem Framing and Modelling
blocks.subtitle: From complaints to measurable problems
blocks.narration: Chapter six. Week four turns observations into work: you will learn to sort facts from opinions, to move from complaint to need to problem statement, to keep the statement solution-free, to choose variables — performance, design, context — and to solve with Need, Know, How, Solve.

blocks.heading: The Elevator Dilemma
bullets: A: design a new elevator
B: increase satisfaction with the elevators
A hides a solution; B keeps options open
blocks.narration: The opening dilemma of lecture four, from the Empire State Building case in Kosky. Workers in a tall office building complain about long elevator waits. Option A: design a new elevator. Option B: increase employee satisfaction with the elevators. Which leaves more options open? B. Formulation A sews the solution into the problem — the complaint was about waiting, yet A forces a new elevator. B admits mirrors by the doors, free coffee on the busiest floors, a new schedule — and only then, if needed, a new elevator. That is exactly how the real Empire State Building case was solved. And a badly framed problem makes us do what we know is wrong.

blocks.heading: Four Kinds of Information
bullets: fact: observed or measured
inference: a conclusion from facts
speculation: a guess, not verified
opinion: a personal view
blocks.narration: When you clarify a problem, everything you hear falls into four categories. A fact is observed or measured — the lunch queue reaches the door at twelve forty, counted. An inference is a conclusion from facts — queues are longest when two class periods end together. A speculation is a guess without evidence — maybe the cashier is the slowest link. An opinion is a personal view — the cafeteria should open a second line. All four are useful: opinions and guesses show what people care about; facts show what is happening. Only facts and good inferences may anchor the statement. The check: hear, observe and measure, then decide — keep what the facts support.

blocks.heading: Sort the Statements
blocks.problem: Classify each statement: fact, inference, speculation, or opinion.

steps.text: A: queues over 15 people, 3 of 5 days — fact
B: 'the cafeteria is badly designed' — opinion
D: 'the cashier is too slow' — opinion

blocks.result: Only facts and inferences anchor the statement
blocks.narration: The lecture's sorting interactive. A: queues exceeded fifteen people on three of five days, counted by a student — a fact, with method and period. B: the cafeteria is badly designed — an opinion, a judgment without evidence. C: queues are longer on soup days — an inference, a pattern read out of observations. D: I think the cashier is too slow — an opinion, a personal view. E: the kitchen probably runs out early — a speculation, a guess about a cause, not verified. F: the average wait was nine minutes at twelve thirty, timed — a fact, with a time and method. The takeaway: only facts and inferences anchor the statement.

blocks.heading: From Complaint to Solution-Free Statement
bullets: complaint — symptom; need — requirement
statement: stakeholder, outcome, measure, limits
no device, app, vehicle, or building in it
blocks.narration: The path runs complaint, need, problem statement. A complaint describes the symptom: we wait too long for the elevators. A need is what the person requires: employees need to reach their floors without exhausting delays. The statement turns need into work: increase employee satisfaction with the elevators. The template: the stakeholder needs the outcome in the system, judged by the measure, within the constraints. And the week's key rule, the solution-free test: no device, no app, no vehicle, no building in the statement. One word can hide a solution. In Kosky's Blimp Wars, the word blimp steered students away from the simple extendable arm. Define the problem in terms of needs, not solutions.

blocks.heading: Rewrite the Problem
blocks.problem: Find the hidden solution and rewrite: (1) build a bigger cafeteria; (2) develop an app showing bus arrival times; (3) install more washing machines.

steps.text: Rewrite: eat without delays, judged by time seated
2. 'An app with bus times' hides an app
Rewrite: know when the next bus arrives

blocks.result: No device, no app, no building named
blocks.narration: The rewrite exercise, with model answers. One: build a bigger cafeteria — the hidden solution is a building. Rewrite: students need to eat without long delays, judged by the time from entering to being seated at peak. Two: an app showing bus times — the hidden solution is an app. Rewrite: passengers need to know when the next bus arrives, judged by the share of passengers able to plan their wait. Three: more washing machines in the laundry — hidden solution: machines. Rewrite: residents need to wash clothes without long waits, judged by the time from arriving to starting the wash. The check in every case is the solution-free test — no device, no app, no building named.

blocks.heading: Three Kinds of Variables
bullets: performance: what we judge the system by
design: the levers we can change
context: the limits we cannot change
blocks.narration: Variables live on the diagram: every step and arrow suggests what can be counted, timed, or weighed. They come in three kinds. Performance variables are what we judge — the average waiting time in minutes, meals per hour, food waste in kilograms per day. Design variables are what we can change — the number of serving lines, staff per shift, the menu size. Context variables are what we cannot change — opening hours, sanitation codes, the building size. The mnemonic: performance is what we judge, design is the levers, context is the limits. And a useful variable answers how many or how much — if you cannot picture how to measure it, keep looking.

blocks.heading: From Vague Words to Variables
blocks.narration: The lecture's table, worth copying into your notes. Crowded becomes the people in the queue — a count. Slow becomes the waiting time at the line — minutes. Wasteful becomes the discarded food — kilograms per day. Expensive becomes the cost per meal — money per meal. Each stakeholder suggests its own measure, too: the rider cares about waiting time at the stop; the driver about the percentage of trips on time; maintenance about breakdowns per month; the administration about cost per passenger; the neighbor about buses per hour on the street. Five perspectives, five performance variables — exactly the link between week three and week four.

blocks.heading: Demands, Wishes and Good Measures
bullets: D: must be met — or the design fails
W: nice to have — not critical
numbers wherever possible
blocks.narration: Specifications come in two marks. A demand, D, must be met — without it the design is unacceptable: every bus passes a safety inspection. A wish, W, is nice to have, not critical: a real-time display at every stop. Two rules: use numbers wherever possible — average peak wait under ten minutes, not short waits — and never turn a wish into a demand; it makes the design harder than needed. A good performance measure shows four signs: measurable, relevant, solution-free, and specific, with units and a target. Beware of averages: the mean wait can look fine while some passengers wait very long — look at the distribution.

blocks.heading: Need, Know, How, Solve
bullets: Need: what we seek — written first
Know: what is given and known
How: the method, with assumptions
Solve: compute, check units, interpret
blocks.narration: Kosky's fail-safe method for solving problems. Need: the variables we are looking for — written down first. Know: the known quantities, from the problem statement or background knowledge — numbers, sketches, principles. How: the solution method, usually an equation, including the assumptions — written before it is applied. Solve: only now compute, check the units, interpret. The payoffs: an audit trail of the solution; a formalized, simpler problem; protection against the temptation to glance and write down the answer; and partial credit even when the answer is wrong. A clear problem statement gives you the Need — the method carries week four into the models of week five.

blocks.heading: The Eight Steps of the Design Process
bullets: define the problem; generate concepts
evaluate and select; detail the design
defend; manufacture and test; evaluate
prepare the final report
blocks.narration: Kosky draws the design process itself as a flow diagram — eight steps. One, define the problem. Two, generate alternative concepts. Three, evaluate and select. Four, detail the design. Five, defend the design. Six, manufacture and test. Seven, evaluate the performance. Eight, prepare the final report. Why systematic? Two goals: eliminate personal biases, and maximize thinking before the design is fixed — fewer iterations, cheaper and faster. Dym's vocabulary completes it: an objective is what we want — adjectives, achievable in part; a constraint is a binary limit — violate it and the design fails; a function is what the device must do, verb plus noun. Unlike a homework problem, a design problem has no unique answer — the best is judged by the client's critical requirements.

items: B beats A: frame the need, not the solution
fact, inference, speculation, opinion

variables: performance, design, context
D must; W nice; numbers always
Need, Know, How, Solve
blocks.narration: Week four in six lines. Increase satisfaction beats design a new elevator — frame the need, not the solution. Sort what you hear into fact, inference, speculation, opinion — only the first two anchor the statement. Use the template: stakeholder, outcome, system, measure, constraints. Variables come as performance, design, and context. Demands must be met, wishes are nice, and numbers go in wherever possible. And solve with Need, Know, How, Solve — the audit trail that earns partial credit.

items: system = elements, processes, inputs, outputs, context
boundary: drawn, not discovered
PFD: 5 symbols, 5 rules, 3 levels
solution-free problem statement
variables + units + significant figures
ethics: canon 1 — safety above all
blocks.narration: Let us put the four weeks together. Engineering is a creative profession that designs before anything breaks, guided by ethics whose first canon is public safety. A system is elements and processes turning inputs into outputs inside an operating context — its boundary drawn, not discovered. The process flow diagram shows steps and flows — five symbols, five rules, three levels. A good problem statement is solution-free and ends in measurable variables. And every calculation runs through Need, Know, How, Solve, with units in brackets and significant figures only at the end. That is the map of weeks one to four.
